hook: Pile drops of water onto a coin and the water bulges into a dome before it spills. Try it eight times and you will not get the same count twice: 31, 28, 33... Which number do you report? Every experiment in this course hits this problem, and four simple numbers solve most of it.

prereq.q: Why can a coin hold a dome of water that rises above its edge?
options: Hydrogen bonds pull surface water molecules toward each other, giving the surface tension.
Covalent bonds form between the water and the metal, gluing the dome in place.
Air pressure pushes down on the dome harder than gravity pulls on it.
prereq.why: Cohesion: water molecules at the surface are pulled inward and sideways by hydrogen bonds to their neighbors, so the surface acts like a stretched skin.

prereq.q: Soap molecules crowd in between water molecules at the surface. What happens to the number of drops the coin can hold?
options: It falls, because fewer hydrogen bonds hold the surface together.
It rises, because soap makes each drop smaller.
It does not change, because soap does not mix with water.
prereq.why: Soap at the surface interrupts hydrogen bonding between water molecules, lowering surface tension, so the dome breaks sooner.

figure.caption: Eight drop counts at 2% soap. Seven sit between 13 and 16; one is 31. The median (15) stays with the cluster, while the mean (16.75) is pulled toward the high value.

chain.cause: You measure the same thing several times (drops on a coin, eight times).
chain.effect: The values differ a little each time, so no single value is "the answer": you have a sample.

chain.cause: You add all eight values and divide by 8.
chain.effect: You get the mean, a center that uses every value, for example 248 ÷ 8 = 31.0 drops.

chain.cause: Because every value adds to the sum, one extreme value (31 among values near 15) adds a lot.
chain.effect: The mean is dragged toward that outlier (16.75 instead of about 14.7).

chain.cause: Sorting the values and taking the middle one (or the average of the middle two) ignores how big the end values are.
chain.effect: The median stays with the cluster (15), so it is the better center when there is an outlier.

chain.cause: Two samples can share a center but differ in how scattered they are.
chain.effect: You also report spread, starting with the range (largest − smallest), to show how consistent the measurements were.

ideas: The mean uses the size of every value; the median uses only position. When a data set has an outlier or is lopsided, the two disagree, and the median describes a typical value better.
Always pair a center with a spread. Two groups with the same mean of 25 drops can have ranges of 2 and 13: the second is far less consistent.
Quantitative data are numbers (counted drops are discrete; measured mass or time are continuous). Qualitative data are categories. You can average numbers, not categories.

misconception.wrong: An outlier is a mistake, so you should delete it before calculating the mean.
misconception.right: An outlier is first checked for a recording or procedure error. If none is found it is real data: keep it, report it, and use the median (which resists it) alongside the mean.

summary: Repeated measurements vary, so you summarize a sample with a center and a spread. The mean (sum ÷ n) uses every value and is pulled by outliers; the median (middle of the sorted data) resists them; the mode is the most common value. The range (largest − smallest) is the simplest measure of spread. Check an outlier for errors before deciding anything about it.
